\textbf{Outlook.} A natural next step is evaluation on openly available empirical contact networks, for example the SocioPatterns high-school contact data \cite{mastrandrea2015} and primary-school contact data \cite{stehle2011,gemmetto2014}. Their class labels provide community partitions, and measured contacts permit comparison of a full-network reference with an interface retaining only $W_{ij}$. Geographically explicit synthetic contact networks also provide individual connections and residential locations, allowing cities or regions to define communities and cross-boundary connections to be aggregated into $W_{ij}$ \cite{jiang2024synthetic}. Alternatively, demographic data and commuting flows can support the construction of local contact networks and aggregate intercommunity weights, provided that the mapping from mobility to contact intensity is explicitly specified \cite{tulchinsky2024networks,tizzoni2014mobility}. A first study could use explicitly defined static contact aggregates; retaining the recorded contact times would require a temporal-network extension. Proper evaluation must address observation windows, contact-weight calibration, incomplete participation, and sensitivity to disease parameters and community definitions. These tasks warrant a dedicated follow-up paper beyond the present methodological study. Such data test fidelity on observed contact structures; validation against observed epidemic outcomes would require additional evidence.

\section{Conclusions}
